title: Union-find
summary: Disjoint sets with near-constant find via path compression and union by rank.

parts.rule: Union-find tracks disjoint sets. Find returns the representative of an element's component. Union merges two components. With path compression and union by rank or size, each operation is amortized nearly constant — growing like the inverse Ackermann function. Use it when connectivity only grows through merges, never splits.
parts.why: Dynamic connectivity and Kruskal-style edge acceptance need something cheaper than rerunning DFS after every added edge. Candidates restart BFS from scratch or nest loops over n. Naming find, union, path compression, and rank is the expected toolkit answer in an algorithms interview.
parts.example: Elements 0 through 5 start as six singleton parents. Union(0,1) attaches 1 under 0. Union(2,3) attaches 3 under 2. Union(1,3) finds representative 0 and representative 2, then attaches 2 under 0 by rank. Now find(3) walks 3 → 2 → 0; path compression can set parent[3]=0 and parent[2]=0 so later finds are flat. Query connected(0,3): both finds return 0 → yes. Query connected(0,4): find(4) is still 4 → no. After three unions you answered connectivity without rebuilding a graph search. In Kruskal you skip an undirected edge when find(u) already equals find(v), because that edge would close a cycle inside one component.
parts.use: Use union-find for connected components under a growing edge set, Kruskal cycle checks, and equivalence classes that only merge. Use it online when edges arrive one at a time and you must answer "same set?" quickly after each merge.
parts.refuse: Refuse union-find when you must split a set again — the structure does not support divide. Refuse it when you need the actual path or distances between nodes; it only answers same-component. Refuse skipping path compression and rank then claiming constant time on large n. Refuse using it as a general shortest-path or BFS substitute.

body:
Rule. Union-find tracks disjoint sets. Find returns the representative of an element's component. Union merges two components. With path compression and union by rank or size, each operation is amortized nearly constant — growing like the inverse Ackermann function. Use it when connectivity only grows through merges, never splits.

Why it matters. Dynamic connectivity and Kruskal-style edge acceptance need something cheaper than rerunning DFS after every added edge. Candidates restart BFS from scratch or nest loops over n. Naming find, union, path compression, and rank is the expected toolkit answer in an algorithms interview.

Worked example. Elements 0 through 5 start as six singleton parents. Union(0,1) attaches 1 under 0. Union(2,3) attaches 3 under 2. Union(1,3) finds representative 0 and representative 2, then attaches 2 under 0 by rank. Now find(3) walks 3 → 2 → 0; path compression can set parent[3]=0 and parent[2]=0 so later finds are flat. Query connected(0,3): both finds return 0 → yes. Query connected(0,4): find(4) is still 4 → no. After three unions you answered connectivity without rebuilding a graph search. In Kruskal you skip an undirected edge when find(u) already equals find(v), because that edge would close a cycle inside one component.

[[diagram:sets]]

When to use. Use union-find for connected components under a growing edge set, Kruskal cycle checks, and equivalence classes that only merge. Use it online when edges arrive one at a time and you must answer "same set?" quickly after each merge.

When to refuse. Refuse union-find when you must split a set again — the structure does not support divide. Refuse it when you need the actual path or distances between nodes; it only answers same-component. Refuse skipping path compression and rank then claiming constant time on large n. Refuse using it as a general shortest-path or BFS substitute.
